papers.title: Small-world networks yield tunable quantum codes at short circuit depth
papers.summary: Monitored random quantum circuits naturally generate quantum error-correcting codes. We generate quantum codes with tunable properties by implementing random Clifford circuits on Watts--Strogatz `small-world' networks and tailor code properties via three knobs: nonlocal graph rewiring, measurement rate, and circuit depth. On fully rewired networks, circuits of logarithmic depth produce codes with a finite rate and an extensive mean contiguous distance with failure probability substantially lower than codes produced from local circuits. These small-world codes form at a circuit depth growing as $\ln n$ compared to polynomial depths required for codes produced from local networks. Rewiring also moves the purification transition to higher measurement rates and changes its critical exponents. Connectivity is thus a knob for designing codes.

papers.title: A Mixed-Methods Study of Personal Software Creation
papers.summary: People have long wanted software shaped around their own data, routines, and preferences. We refer to such software as \emph{personal software}. For decades, programming expertise limited who could build it: people without that expertise could build software only within constrained end-user programming tools, such as spreadsheets. AI coding agents seem to remove this bottleneck by letting people build full applications from natural-language descriptions, and many people now build and share personal software publicly. Yet personal software has rarely been studied at scale: we know little about what people build and why, how they build it, and what opportunities and challenges they encounter. We investigate these questions with a mixed-methods study. A grey-literature review examines 6,168 web and Reddit posts, and an observation study follows eight people as they build software for their own needs with AI coding agents and use it for up to a week. We find that creators value personal software for how closely it fits a particular person or community. The software takes shape as creators react to what the agent builds: most functionality emerged during building, and creators' effort shifted from writing code to checking it.

papers.title: Advancing the Theory of Pretty Good Quantum Operations
papers.summary: Finding optimal quantum measurements or recovery maps is often demanding. Pretty good measurements and Petz maps offer explicit approximations achieving at least the square of optimal performance by the Barnum-Knill bound. We unify these operations in a semidefinite programming framework with a tunable power, extending them to broader quantum tasks. We prove a stronger bound for powers above one up to three that peaks at quadratic power. For structured channels such as stabilizer codes under Pauli noise, large powers steer recovery to a maximum likelihood decoder for maximally mixed inputs.

papers.title: ACAP: Asynchronous Coding Agents for Efficient Robot Control
papers.summary: Coding agents can construct and revise robot behavior during execution, but using one agent for the whole robot can delay otherwise independent work. We introduce Asynchronous Coding Agents as Policy (ACAP), an asynchronous framework that organizes one robot as a team of persistent agents. Each member reasons and acts for a configurable control group, such as an arm with its gripper or the torso and chassis, enabling asynchronous reasoning and execution. However, different robot components often have physical dependencies that require coordination. To address this challenge, ACAP introduces a hyper-agent that assigns tasks, coordinates dependencies, and dynamically allocates control between the lead and member agents. This allows independent work to progress concurrently while supporting tightly coupled manipulation when necessary. Across 72 real-world rollouts covering 25 task/platform settings, ACAP reduces task-balanced time cost by 28.2% compared with a single-agent Direct Policy, with improvements across Fully Parallel, Parallel-Sequential, and Collaborative tasks. Across all eight Collaborative settings, ACAP also achieves lower mean time cost than Fixed Delegation, where only member agents can control their assigned groups. An additional 90-rollout study shows lower mean 30-minute-capped time cost than Direct on all six tasks. We further demonstrate mobile manipulation using the same member interface for chassis and torso control. We present the framework and a real-world rollout dataset containing observations, generated programs, actions, and feedback to support research on how coding agents reason and act in the physical world.

papers.title: ToolSmith: An Automatic Tool-Generation Framework for Multimodal Search Agents
papers.summary: Recent multimodal search agents use reasoning, vision, and live web search across many turns to answer questions beyond parametric knowledge by orchestrating a small library of hand-crafted search and visual tools. However, the library is laborious to create and maintain, and frozen when new query types, evidence formats, and failure modes are encountered in the wild. Human practitioners, by contrast, cope with insufficient tools by fashioning new ones from familiar parts and reusing them across tasks. Inspired by this, we propose ToolSmith, an automatic tool-generation framework that grows and reuses modules on top of a lean base tool library. We evaluate ToolSmith on three in-domain multimodal search benchmarks and ten out-of-domain benchmarks under a VLM-as-a-Judge protocol. ToolSmith consistently improves over the base library across deployed agents of varying scales, with larger backbones reaping greater gains, demonstrating the scalability of the approach. Our code and data are available at https://threesr.github.io/toolsmith/.

papers.title: Learning Neurovascular Codes for EEG-to-fMRI Synthesis
papers.summary: In this paper, we introduce Neurovascular Codes as shared EEG representations for fMRI generation. We first train a separate EEG encoder to predict each fMRI signal, learning target-specific temporal and spectral features from the same EEG window. After training, we freeze the encoders and project their concatenated hidden features into a shared neurovascular code. Conditioned on this code, stochastic interpolant transforms Gaussian noise into a vector of fMRI signals, allowing different responses to be sampled for the same EEG window. We evaluate our approach on eight public simultaneous EEG-fMRI datasets, including four resting-state and four task-based datasets with 61,646 volume-level pairs. Under within-subject and held-out-subject evaluation, our model improves average Pearson correlation over the strongest encoder baselines by 19.1% and 19.8%, respectively. The corresponding improvements over the strongest generator baselines are 18.8% and 47.9%. Beyond reconstruction accuracy, we also evaluate the generated signals using subject-identification classifiers trained on real fMRI. Our method achieves the highest mean accuracy among the evaluated generators. We hope that our work opens up new opportunities for cross-modal brain modeling.

papers.title: Probabilistic, facility-specific prioritisation of temperate exoplanets for atmospheric characterisation with JWST and the ELT
papers.summary: Deciding which temperate exoplanets to observe first matters for JWST transit spectroscopy and for planned ELT reflected-light instruments, yet signal-to-noise metrics ignore habitability and similarity indices ignore observability. We present an open Monte Carlo framework (UHI v6.1) that builds probabilistic priority lists separately for each facility and composition class, never as a single ranking. For each of 6,112 planets in the NASA Exoplanet Archive, 10,000 draws carry catalogue uncertainties through climate, cumulative stellar-XUV atmospheric retention, per-draw rocky, Hycean or gas-rich classes, and a JWST (transiting) or ELT/PCS (non-transiting) detection model, giving each planet a survival probability, a conditional score and a top-N probability. At $5σ$, 255 rocky and 71 Hycean candidates remain viable. A Saltelli--Sobol analysis of 32 assumptions ($N = 512$) shows that the location and width of the XUV shoreline dominate the rocky lists, with total-order indices of 0.22 and 0.12 at $5σ$ (0.25 and 0.14 at $3σ$), and all ten leading indices have 95% bootstrap half-widths below 0.05. For Hycean planets most outputs are degenerate and the analysis does not converge, so that branch is reported as indicative. Membership of these lists is limited mainly by whether a planet survives the habitability vetoes: at $5σ$, 3 of the nominal JWST and 4 of the nominal ELT rocky top-10 targets enter the top 10 in at least half of all draws, yet every one of them stays in the top 10 in more than half of the draws in which it survives. Code, per-planet posterior summaries, sensitivity tables and maps are public, so observers can rerun the lists under their own instrument assumptions and see which inputs would most change a target's priority.

papers.title: Code-Based Message Authentication with Statistical Guarantees via Coordinate Selection and Masking
papers.summary: We study message authentication over a public channel against a computationally unbounded adversary. Motivated by low-complexity applications, we consider schemes that leverage off-the-shelf binary linear codes already used for error correction in communication systems. Existing code-based constructions derive an authentication tag primarily from a single symbol in a $q$-ary code, which limits the tag length. However, selecting several binary coordinates allows a fixed binary linear code to support different tag lengths. We characterize how coordinate selection and ordering affect the statistical guarantees against impersonation and substitution attacks. In particular, we explore three methods: the subset selector, the ordered selector, and the independent selector. They read uniformly chosen coordinates in a fixed public or a secret random order, or with replacement, and add a uniform mask. With a fresh key per message, all three achieve the optimal impersonation probability $2^{-l_t}$ for $l_t$-bit tags. We bound the subset selector's substitution probability using only nonzero weights. Those of the other two depend only on the code length $n$, $l_t$, and the nonzero weight farthest from $n/2$. The independent selector achieves $2^{-l_t}$ for substitution when all nonzero weights equal $n/2$. Finally, we evaluate first-order Reed-Muller and Bose-Chaudhuri-Hocquenghem dual subcodes.

papers.title: Female YouTube Content Creators in Bangladesh: A Data-Driven Study of Audience and Sentiment
papers.summary: Audience response to female-led YouTube channels in Bangladesh has not been measured at scale, and the comments these channels attract are hard to score because they arrive in three different writing systems. This study examines twelve such channels, two per category across six categories, from January 2021 to August 2026, covering 4,717 videos and a census of 558,827 top-level comments. No single writing system dominates the comment set: English accounts for 33.5%, Bangla script for 32.0%, and Banglish (Bengali typed in Latin script and freely mixed with English) for 24.2%. Each comment was therefore routed to a model trained on the language it was actually written in rather than translated into English. Two categories, selected for the largest rise and the largest drop in positive sentiment over time, were hand-labeled and used to fine-tune the code-mixed model, raising out-of-fold accuracy from 54.3% to 78.0% in Health & Fitness and from 81.1% to 85.0% in Beauty & Fashion, and moving the first category's reported positive share by nearly eight points. The wider results show diverging publishing trends, highly concentrated audience attention, category-specific sentiment trajectories, and a clean split between event-like and search-driven categories in how quickly audiences respond. The findings underscore that language-aware sentiment analysis is essential for Bangladeshi social media data, that even a language-appropriate general model can be systematically miscalibrated for a specific community, and that measured negative shares are best read as lower bounds.

papers.title: SPROUT: Predicting Objective-Grounded Prompt Utility for Efficient Text-to-Image Preference Tuning
papers.summary: Preference tuning of text-to-image diffusion models spends most of its compute generating candidate images, yet training prompts are typically sampled uniformly at random, wasting compute generating images that provide too little signal for model alignment. To best utilize the available compute, we study prompt selection, where at each iteration we identify the most useful prompts for preference tuning. We separate prompt selection into a utility score, an estimator of that utility score, and batch selection. Within this framework, we propose Selection by PRedicting Objective-grounded UTility (SPROUT). The utility score is predicted on every prompt in the pool, including unseen prompts, by a text-only model, refit after every iteration on all utilities observed so far. A randomized acceptance rule then turns these predictions into a batch, so no images are generated beyond those used for training. For direct group preference optimization (DGPO), the objective-grounded utility is the norm of the gradient that the objective produces from a prompt's group of images. Fine-tuning Stable Diffusion 1.5 with DGPO on GenEval, SPROUT matches the final score of uniform sampling in about 44% of the iterations and improves the area under the learning curve with respect to both uniform sampling and CGPO, a recent variance-based prompt sampler. The efficiency gains hold under four held-out reward models never used in training, and the ranking of methods carries over to DPG-Bench and T2I-CompBench++. Our code is available at https://github.com/ADDAPT-ML/SPROUT.

papers.title: Shaderous: A Browser-based Hydrodynamics Code for Physics Research and Teaching
papers.summary: Shaderous is a three-dimensional code for compressible gas dynamics and magnetohydrodynamics that runs in WebGPU compute shaders in a web browser on any vendor's GPU. It combines an unsplit MUSCL-Hancock scheme and HLLC fluxes with a multigrid Poisson solver, block-structured adaptive mesh refinement with per-block timesteps, constrained transport with HLLD fluxes, point masses with sinks, gray radiation transport with the M1 closure, implicit pressure for low Mach numbers, tabulated equations of state from degenerate electrons to rock and iron, cooling, viscosity, conduction, resistivity, mixtures of gases, and nuclear burning by a neural network trained on a 13-isotope reaction network. A setup is shared as a link and runs on a student's own laptop or phone, so the code suits teaching at every level. A run is limited to one GPU: the largest adaptive mesh so far held about 175 million cells on an NVIDIA H200. It therefore suits parameter studies, run as sweeps from the command line, rather than the largest single simulations. Three aspects of the design are, as far as we can find, new. First, the hydrodynamic solver stores no face flux. The two cells that share a face compute bit-identical fluxes, so cells at boundaries between levels and between timesteps recompute their neighbors' fluxes instead of keeping a flux register. Mass, momentum and energy are conserved to round-off on the adaptive mesh, and compensated sums keep the divergence of the magnetic field at round-off. Second, the whole step runs on the GPU: the timestep and the assignment of blocks to time bins are reduced there, and ghost cells are computed as they are loaded rather than exchanged. Third, the code computes in single precision yet reproduces a range of astrophysical systems accurately, from stars and atmospheres in hydrostatic balance to shocks, gravitational collapse and magnetized flows, in 206 validation tests.

papers.title: Head Anything: Correspondence-Guided Joint Generation of 3D Heads from Few Images
papers.summary: Large image-to-3D generators recover detailed heads from a single photograph but treat every image as a new object. For several images of one person, they hallucinate unseen regions independently without using information from the other images. We present Head Anything, which generates detailed head meshes from a few images with changing expressions and viewpoints. Instead of training a multi-image prior, we turn a pretrained single-image generator with a native 3D latent space into a joint generator that denoises all images together. Since global attention between images is hard to learn from scarce 3D head data, lightweight correspondence-attention adapters let every 3D token attend only to its corresponding points in the other images. We obtain correspondences by fitting a neural parametric head model to the generator's own single-image outputs, requiring no ground truth at test time. Training on both ground-truth and fitted correspondences makes the adapters robust to fitting errors. Each mesh stays pixel-aligned with its own image and borrows the unseen regions from all others. On head scans, Head Anything lowers the head Chamfer distance of the best image-to-3D generator by 32% and its cross-frame inconsistency by 47%, and its meshes improve face tracking. Code and models will be released.

papers.title: HoloSplat: Real-Time Token Streaming for Feed-Forward Human Reconstruction
papers.summary: Live free-viewpoint video streaming of humans enables immersive telepresence and interactive XR applications. However, this requires reconstructing each frame in real time, transmitting the data within strict bandwidth budgets, and decoding it on lightweight client GPUs. Existing approaches, whether relying on per-frame optimization or feed-forward inference, generate massive 3D Gaussian payloads that exceed practical streaming limits, while aggressive compression severely degrades rendering quality. In this work, we present HoloSplat, a real-time streaming framework for human-centric volumetric video. HoloSplat splits a feed-forward reconstructor before its Gaussian head, introducing a multi-rate streaming codec driven by server-side token compression and client-side token restoration. On the server side, we apply opacity-guided token pruning, PCA-based dimensionality reduction, and lossless geometry coding for token anchors. On the client side, a feature reconstruction hypernetwork is fused into the Gaussian head to recover compression-induced quality loss. Furthermore, we introduce Neural Session Calibration (NSC), which rapidly fine-tunes the Gaussian head online using incoming camera views during a warm-up phase. This resolves quality degradation from novel camera parameters and varying capture conditions with zero per-frame overhead. In our evaluations, HoloSplat averages 32.2 FPS on four RTX 5090 GPUs at 50 Mbit/s. It decodes each frame into 3D Gaussians in 22.1 ms on an RTX 3050 Ti laptop GPU, transmitting 22.8$\times$ less data than uncompressed float32 Gaussians, while calibrated decoding improves PSNR by 1.050 dB.

papers.title: Attention Temperature Confounds Zero-Shot Context Extension
papers.summary: A training-time attention change is usually judged for zero-shot context extension against a dense baseline beyond the training length at the default temperature, $τ= 1$. The outcome depends on how miscalibrated the baseline is there: the share of perplexity it recovers when its logits are sharpened by one scalar. Under the standard recipe (fp32 master weights), an 8k-trained baseline is 8-15% miscalibrated at 30k in three seed-paired 365M twins; in one of them this makes the block-sparse-trained twin look 7% better, which calibration removes. In pure-bf16 training without master weights the miscalibration is several times larger: an AdamW step ($β_2 = 0.95$) on a gain initialised at 1.0 is below half the bf16 spacing at peak learning rates under $1.7\times10^{-3}$, so gains never move (22 checkpoints), the baseline is 37-58% miscalibrated, and block-sparse pretraining, attention dropout and ALiBi look 6-35% better. Calibrating one temperature per model and length removes all three advantages, leaves ALiBi 5% behind RoPE and keeps part of the gain of a positive control, NTK-aware scaling. Unfreezing the gains reverses the block-sparse advantage at 365M and removes 71-89% of it at 1.2B. We recommend reporting extension results at calibrated temperatures and checking that normalisation gains moved.

papers.title: Look Back, Draft Ahead: Corrective Prefix Attention for Parallel Speculative Decoding
papers.summary: Parallel speculative decoders propose an entire token block at once, yet one early inconsistency can cause the target to reject its remaining suffix. We introduce Corrective Prefix Attention (CPA), which combines prefix-aware selection with autoregressive supervision to improve these parallel drafts. CPA lets each candidate attend to earlier choices within the block. Fixed candidate shortlists allow all pairwise interactions to be computed before selection, reducing the sequential walk to table lookups, accumulation and lightweight scoring rather than repeated neural evaluations. An auxiliary autoregressive loss trains the shared backbone on clean prefixes without adding an inference pass. Across eight math, code and dialogue benchmarks with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B targets on Ascend NPUs, CPA commits 13--15\% more tokens per verification round than DSpark and 25--26\% more than DFlash. Its mean speedups reach $3.35\times$ and $3.37\times$ under greedy decoding and $2.86\times$ under sampling for both targets. Ablations support both components, while capacity sweeps demonstrate that greater acceptance alone does not guarantee faster decoding. These results motivate correcting parallel proposals with causal information while keeping sequential computation inexpensive.

papers.title: CASPER: Discovering Spatially Resolved Causal Cell-Cell Communications
papers.summary: Spatial transcriptomics can reveal where ligands and receptors are expressed together. A harder question is whether exposure to a ligand changes pathway activity in nearby cells, since the same tissue environment can influence both ligand expression and pathway activity. We introduce CASPER, a Bayesian structural equation model that adjusts for receptor expression and represents the shared tissue environment with a Gaussian Markov random field. We show that the ligand-exposure effect is identifiable when the spatial covariance is known and distinguishable from independent noise, the coefficients are constant, and the structural errors are independent and homoskedastic. In simulations, CASPER reduced the bias seen in ordinary regression and in a regression that accounted for spatial dependence only in the outcome. We compared CASPER with CellPhoneDB in four public Xenium datasets. In ovarian cancer, CellPhoneDB found evidence of ligand--receptor expression enrichment for both IL6 and VEGFA. CASPER found greater support for a positive effect of fibroblast IL6 on the inflammatory-response score of ciliated epithelial cells than for an effect of fibroblast VEGFA on the angiogenesis score of endothelial cells. Code accompanies the Supplementary Materials and is available at https://github.com/nySTAT/casperCCC.

papers.title: Orthogonally Mixed Sign Coding with Progressive Residual Refinement for Transformer Weight Compression
papers.summary: LLM quantization reduces storage but often degrades predictive fidelity at low bit rates. We propose a training-free, CDF-free, Gaussian-CLT-motivated progressive residual-sign quantization framework that uses randomized orthogonal mixing to promote Gaussian-like residual distributions and improve sign based reconstruction of Transformer weights. Each stage independently normalizes residuals and analytically calibrates reconstruction, progressively recovering quantization errors. The framework enables flexible storage-fidelity trade-offs without learned codebooks, empirical CDFs, or trellis optimization. We evaluate GPT-2 Large and Llama-3-8B across attention and MLP projections. At five residual stages, joint quantization preserves near-baseline predictive fidelity, achieving perplexities of 32.16 and 12.73, compared with full-precision values of 29.89 and 11.07, respectively. Ablations further demonstrate that orthogonal mixing substantially improves reconstruction over identity-based sign coding, while activation-aware scaling improves output fidelity and reduced-precision statistics lower storage overhead with negligible perplexity degradation. Comparisons with conventional quantizers establish the method's progressive fidelity recovery and characterize its storage-quality and runtime trade-offs. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of orthogonally mixed residual-sign coding for flexible, training-free Transformer weight compression.

papers.title: AI-Assisted Programming and Labor Demand
papers.summary: Generative AI has demonstrated human-level performance on technical work tasks, yet evidence on how these task-level capabilities are changing labor demand remains scarce. We study the firm-level adoption of GitHub Copilot, an AI coding assistant, across 5,414 multinational firms accounting for 38% of the U.S. programming workforce. To identify causal effects, we exploit a natural experiment generated by firms' predetermined software procurement cycles. Early AI-adopting firms hired more workers before the launch of GitHub Copilot and had larger, more technical, and older workforces. After one year, GitHub Copilot adoption reduces quarterly technical hiring by 29% among review-induced adopters, with no effect on separations, overall technical headcount, or vacancy duration. The hiring slowdown is concentrated in the subset of junior technical roles that involve the highest share of coding work. Overall, AI coding assistance causes firms to shift demand towards more experienced workers and roles that pair some coding with broader design responsibilities.

papers.title: UMAMI: A Multimodal Benchmark Dataset for Evidence-Grounded Dietary Decisions
papers.summary: Dietary decisions require identifying a food's nutrient content and considering individual dietary needs, but recognizing food from an image alone does not provide this information. Visually similar foods can have different nutrient profiles, so selecting the wrong food record can lead to incorrect decisions even when nutrient rules are applied correctly. Furthermore, satisfying nutrient constraints does not necessarily establish a food's relevance to a person's intake. Evaluating these challenges together requires connecting food images, nutrient records, and individual intake histories. To support this evaluation, we introduce UMAMI (Unified Multimodal Assessment of Meals and Intake), a multimodal dataset and benchmark linking independently collected food images with nutrient profiles and respondent health and intake records. Using this dataset, we construct three diagnostic tasks covering visual nutrient question answering, personalized food recommendation, and condition-aware food substitution. Paired instances and input controls examine how visual identity and respondent context affect decisions. Our experiments identify errors in both food-record selection and nutrient-rule application, while showing that higher rule compliance does not necessarily improve alignment with subsequent recorded intake. These findings highlight the need to evaluate how multimodal systems select and use structured evidence for dietary decisions. The dataset, code, and dashboard are available at https://umami-benchmark.github.io.

papers.title: ReWeave: Emergent Physical Task Topologies for Embodied Harness Optimization and Cross-Task Meta-Distillation
papers.summary: Long-horizon embodied tasks involve physical dependencies that may only become clear through interaction. As task understanding deepens, past trials can reveal new information for adaptation and transfer. However, coarse progress feedback cannot identify which physical preconditions held, leaving search unguided, while task-specific optimization easily overfits to individual scenes, making cross-task transfer brittle. We introduce ReWeave, a framework that jointly optimizes an embodied agent harness and an emergent physical task topology from interaction without updating policy weights. Keeping execution policies and perception frozen, ReWeave co-optimizes coupled context, workflows, and control loops. As new evidence revises the topology, ReWeave reprojects past trials onto the updated task understanding, exposing retained progress, regressions, and bottlenecks that guide parent selection and search width. Across tasks, matching verified local mechanisms to unmet preconditions consolidates 72 specialist units into 44 reusable groups ($0.34\times$ full concatenation) within a compact shared harness capable of continual learning. ReWeave improves held-out success from 89.00% to 98.75% on LIBERO-PRO and from 25.50% to 58.25% on RoboDojo, while uncovering retained progress in 89% of 159 failed RoboDojo development trials and translating stronger offline reasoning into higher online performance. On eight unseen LIBERO-PRO tasks, the shared harness reaches 51.3% success versus 41.3% for direct distillation, rising to 75.0% after continual learning.
